question_text:
Assuming that the conductivity for copper in Table is entirely due to free electrons [with a mobility of $3.5 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~m}^{2} /(\mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{s})$ ], calculate the density of free electrons in copper at room temperature. 

Refer to Table:
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline \multicolumn{3}{|c|}{Electrical Conductivities of Some Materials at Room Temperature} \\
\hline Conducting range & Material & Conductivity, $\sigma\left(\Omega^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{m}^{-1}\right)$ \\
\hline \multirow[t]{4}{*}{Conductors} & Aluminum (annealed) & $35.36 \times 10^6$ \\
\hline & Copper (annealed standard) & $58.00 \times 10^6$ \\
\hline & Iron (99.99 + \%) & $10.30 \times 10^6$ \\
\hline & Steel (wire) & $5.71-9.35 \times 10^6$ \\
\hline \multirow[t]{3}{*}{Semiconductors} & Germanium (high purity) & 2.0 \\
\hline & Silicon (high purity) & $0.40 \times 10^{-3}$ \\
\hline & Lead sulfide (high purity) & 38.4 \\
\hline \multirow[t]{4}{*}{Insulators} & Aluminum oxide & $10^{-10}-10^{-12}$ \\
\hline & Borosilicate glass & $10^{-13}$ \\
\hline & Polyethylene & $10^{-13}-10^{-15}$ \\
\hline & Nylon 66 & $10^{-12}-10^{-13}$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}The unit of the answer is mathrm{~m}^{-3}.
